stimulus:
Let it be admitted at the outset that European brains, capital, and energy have not been, and never will be, expended in developing the resources of Africa from motives of pure philanthropy; that Europe is in Africa for the mutual benefit of her own industrial classes, and of the native races in their progress to a higher plane; that the benefit can be made reciprocal, and that it is the aim and desire of civilised administration to fulfil this dual mandate.

By railways and roads, by reclamation of swamps and irrigation of deserts, and by a system of fair trade and competition, we have added to the prosperity and wealth of these lands, and checked famine and disease. We have put an end to the awful misery of the slave trade and inter-tribal war, to human sacrifice and the ordeals of the witch-doctor. Where these things survive they are severely suppressed. We are endeavouring to teach the native races to conduct their own affairs with justice and humanity, and to educate them alike in letters and in industry. . . . Liberty and justice have replaced chaos, bloodshed, and war.

—Frederick Lugard, British colonial administrator, excerpt from 
The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa
, 1922

Our policy is one of heart and reason, duty and [economic] interests. [We must aim for] an equilibrium of the power of sentiment and the power of interest. . . . If government were placed in the hands of the natives, disorder and incoherence, and then anarchy, revolt, and the rending of the entire country’s social fabric would result. . . . Although we are perhaps less generous than other [colonizing] nations in the verbal liberalism of constitutions granted, we compensate for this parsimony in political “rights” with a sincere tenderness toward the colonial peoples.

—Albert Sarraut, French colonial administrator, excerpt from 
The Improvement of the French Colonies
, 1923
stem: What does the first author most likely mean when he writes of a “dual mandate”?
options: (A) Imperial powers ought to use their colonies to increase wealth not only for their business elites but also for their ordinary citizens.
(B) Colonial administrations must foster economic growth as well as tend to the task of military defense.
(C) European governments can and should pursue colonial rule in ways that will benefit both the colonizers and the colonized.
(D) Colonial populations must be sharply segregated, with natives subject to a different and stricter set of rules than the colonizers.
explanation: Any colonial administrator of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries would have agreed with (A) and (B), so defining a special concept like the “dual mandate” would not be necessary to express these ideas. The rigid distinctions between class and especially race referred to in (D), with social and legal privileges reserved for white colonists, was very much the rule in European possessions abroad, but this separation is not the duality Lugard has in mind. In a paternalist way that was common among Westerners during the late 1800s and much of the 1900s, Lugard has convinced himself that colonization, properly done, can be made to work for the good of those being colonized, who are able to strive toward a “higher plane” under the “guidance” of “more civilized” Europeans. This notion that one can serve one’s own interests and simultaneously “uplift” those one is taking advantage of is at the heart of (C), the correct response.

stem: Which of the following statements would both authors be MOST likely to agree with?
options: (A) Racial superiority entitles white colonists to exploit their non-white colonial subjects to whatever extent they please.
(B) Although an obvious injustice, colonization is an unavoidable necessity if European economies are to remain healthy.
(C) Native peoples, incapable of governing themselves at present, benefit from benevolent rule by European colonizers.
(D) In light of new twentieth-century values concerning racial equality, colonial regimes should be dismantled as soon as possible.
explanation: All four of these views had supporters during the twentieth century, although some were older and some newer. Answer (A) refers to an older view that would have been more common in the 1800s but still had adherents in the 1900s, although it is more hard-edged that what Lugard and Sarraut have to say, at least in principle. Answer (D) states an actively anti-colonial position that would have been more typical of later decades and does not match either man’s thinking at all. Answer (B) would apply to people during the 1920s, but Lugard and Sarraut do not voice any of the reluctance or regret about colonization one would expect if (B) truly summarized their views. Instead, both were inspired by the condescending idea of “benevolent” imperialism—as discussed in the answer to the previous question—making (C) correct.

stem: Which of the following most closely matches the attitudes expressed by the authors of the passages above?
options: (A) White Man’s Burden
(B) Marxism-Leninism
(C) Social Darwinism
(D) Neocolonialism
explanation:
This question puts a label on the attitude examined by the first two questions. All of these concepts were relevant to the topic of colonization in the late 1800s and/or 1900s. However, Marxism-Leninism (which claimed to be in favor of liberating colonies from imperialist capitalist powers) would hardly have informed the mindset of French or British colonial officials, and although social Darwinism remained a common justification for imperialism in the early 1900s, Lugard and Sarraut do not appear to have favored this nakedly competitive view nearly as much as they did the condescendingly “benevolent” understanding of imperialism—all of which makes (A) (the phrase coined by the British poet Rudyard Kipling) a better answer than (B) or (C). Neocolonialism refers to the more indirect ways that Western nations exert influence on the less developed world 
after
 decolonization, without the direct imposition of political authority, so (D) belongs to later decades and does not describe the straightforward colonization that Lugard and Sarraut were involved with.

stem: In what way do the two authors’ ideas most differ?
options: (A) The first author conveys a greater willingness to put down native resistance with military force.
(B) The second author is less disposed to share responsibility for political affairs with a colony’s native population.
(C) The first author argues for a greater degree of economic control over his country’s colonies.
(D) The second author implies a greater sympathy for the work of Christian missionaries in Asia and Africa.
explanation: Both Lugard and Sarraut have similar views about colonial administration, so any differences between them are likely to be subtle. Both would have felt justified in using force against any natives who threatened colonial authority, and both were equally concerned with running colonies profitably, so (A) and (C) are not good places to look for gaps between the two men’s thinking. On the whole, French colonial officials were more inclined than their British counterparts to support Christian missionary work, but Sarraut says nothing about this topic in the given passage, so one cannot assume that (D) is true. While Lugard speaks of “teach[ing] the native races to conduct their own affairs,” Sarraut explicitly refers to the “parsimony,” or stinginess, with which he feels political rights should be doled out by colonizing powers, making (B) correct.

stem: The factor contributing to the rise in carbon dioxide levels, as measured in the second of the above charts, is believed by most scientists to be caused by
options: (A) gradual acidification of the world’s oceans.
(B) the burning of fossil fuels.
(C) global intensification of factory farming.
(D) natural fluctuations in the climate.
explanation:
All of these answers refer to developments that have emerged in recent decades. Answer (A) describes an 
effect
 (brought about, in fact, by the same trend resulting in the carbon dioxide rise that the chart measures), rather than a 
cause
, so it can be ignored. Climate shifts do occur naturally, but contrary to the rhetoric of climate change deniers, these shifts unfold over time scales measured in thousands of years, and not fast enough to cause the change shown in the chart; (D) is therefore incorrect. Agricultural activities can contribute to carbon emissions but not nearly as directly or in the same quantities as the burning of coal, gas, and oil, so (C) is wrong by comparison with (B), an answer supported by overwhelming scientific consensus.

stem: Which of the following best summarizes the correlation between the two charts shown above?
options: (A) Increased energy consumption appears to be a likely cause of rising carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere.
(B) There appears to be no meaningful correlation between the two charts.
(C) The developing world appears to bear greater responsibility than the developed world for the production of greenhouse gases.
(D) International agreements to slow the pace of climate change appear to have substantially curbed greenhouse gas emissions.
explanation: Leaving aside the question of whether to count China as part of the developed or developing world, the United States by itself consumes enough energy that (C) cannot be correct (if Europe’s consumption were measured by the first chart, this fact would be even clearer). The sharp rise of carbon dioxide levels noted on the second chart directly contradicts (D), and the curves on both charts correspond so closely to each other that one needs no outside knowledge about current climate trends to know that (B) is false. The causal link between fossil fuel consumption—which continues apace, especially as parts of the developing world modernize fully—and the production of greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide is an established fact, as indicated by (A).

stimulus: (Left) Paul Plaschke, cartoon depicting the Yalta Conference, early 1945; (right) Clifford K. Berryman, “Path to Peace,” August 1946
stem: The two cartoons above are MOST concerned with which of the following topics?
options: (A) The threat of atomic war in the years following World War II
(B) The construction of the Berlin Wall and similarly strict border crossings
(C) The formation of superpower spheres of influence during the early Cold War
(D) The triumph of communism in mainland China
explanation: All four of these concerns arose during the Cold War. However, the Berlin Wall was not built until 1961, and the USSR did not possess atomic weapons until 1949 (furthermore, while the cartoons depict a conflictual relationship, neither contains a sense of immediate military alarm). Answers (A) and (B) are therefore weaker bets. While China is referred to in the Plaschke cartoon, the main emphasis appears to be Stalin’s acquisition of Europe, in the form of poker chips won during the metaphorical card game, and the second cartoon deals exclusively with Europe, making (D) less relevant. In the Plaschke cartoon, the USSR is shown as having outmaneuvered the West on the question of territorial concessions at the Yalta Conference, where the post–World War II fate of central and Eastern Europe was determined, and the Shepherd cartoon depicts the West and the USSR as competing for influence in the Balkans. Both align closely with (C).

stimulus: (Left) Paul Plaschke, cartoon depicting the Yalta Conference, early 1945; (right) Clifford K. Berryman, “Path to Peace,” August 1946
stem: Which of the following documents would be most relevant to the concerns raised by both cartoons?
options: (A) Sukarno’s opening address to the Bandung Conference of non-aligned states
(B) Nikita Khrushchev’s “secret speech” to the Twentieth Party Congress
(C) Dwight Eisenhower’s “military-industrial complex” farewell address
(D) Winston Churchill’s “iron curtain” speech at Westminster College
explanation: All four of these speeches touched upon Cold War realities. Those referred to in (A), (B), and (C) came later than the period depicted in the cartoons (1955, 1956, and 1961, respectively), but even if you do not know these dates, the subjects do not square precisely with that of the cartoons. Sukarno, in (A), hoped to avoid the spheres of influence the cartoons allude to; Khrushchev, in (B), focused on de-Stalinizing Soviet domestic politics; and Eisenhower, in (C), was more directly concerned with the implications of the Cold War arms race. It was Churchill who famously associated the Soviet domination of Eastern Europe immediately after World War II with the metaphor of the “iron curtain,” as in answer (D).

stimulus:
We organize to initiate or support action to break through the silken curtain of prejudice and discrimination against women in government, industry, the professions, the churches, the political parties, the judiciary, the labor unions, in education, science, medicine, law, religion and every other field of importance in American society. Enormous changes taking place in our society make it both possible and urgently necessary to advance the unfinished revolution of women toward true equality, now. With a life span lengthened to nearly 75 years it is no longer either necessary or possible for women to devote the greater part of their lives to child-rearing; yet childbearing and rearing which continues to be a most important part of most women’s lives—still is used to justify barring women from equal professional and economic participation and advance.

Today’s women once performed in the home and in mass-production industries based upon routine unskilled labor. This same technology has virtually eliminated the quality of muscular strength as a criterion for filling most jobs, while intensifying American industry’s need for creative intelligence. In view of this new industrial revolution created by automation in the mid-twentieth century, women can and must participate in old and new fields of society in full equality—or become permanent outsiders.

— “Statement of Purpose,” issued upon the founding of the National Organization of Women (NOW), Washington, D.C., October 1966
stem: The views expressed in this document would be MOST ideologically compatible with those of
options: (A) Margaret Thatcher.
(B) Simone de Beauvoir.
(C) Frida Kahlo.
(D) Nancy Reagan.
explanation: Although all four of the women in this list were high-achieving and influential, whether culturally or politically, one lesson from the history of gender and sexuality is that not all women who attain status or power are actively concerned or involved with advancing the cause of gender equality. Answers (A) and (D) refer to politically powerful women (prime minister of Great Britain in Thatcher’s case, prominent U.S. First Lady in Reagan’s) whose conservative outlooks left them indifferent, if not hostile, to maximum efforts on behalf of women’s equality, at least as embodied by groups like the National Organization for Women. The Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, answer (C), had much to say in her work about gender roles and patriarchy, and many of her views would have been in tune with NOW’s, but it is Simone de Beauvoir, answer (B), who played the most direct role in the shaping of feminist thought in the 1900s and who, in fact, directly inspired the generation of the 1960s who framed the NOW statement.

stem: Which of the following best summarizes how the above document compares to the main thrust of feminist thinking in the late 1800s and early 1900s?
options: (A) The later strain of thought aspired to move beyond basic rights, such as voting, to equality in as many spheres as possible.
(B) The later strain of thought rejected the accomplishments associated with the earlier one as too inadequate.
(C) The later strain of thought was much less strongly influenced by Marxist ideology than the earlier one.
(D) Women’s rights had advanced little enough that the two strains of thought remained essentially the same.
explanation: While later waves of feminist thought have generally sought to expand and build on earlier efforts, outright rejection, as in (B), has not been the case, and while full equality is not yet in sight, enough has changed to make (D) false.
